Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists: Political organization. The OUN was mostly active preceding, during, and immediately after the Second World War.

Beginning with the rise of Augustus in 27 BC and ending with the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 AD, this roughly 200-year golden age saw the empire reach its greatest territorial extent under Trajan — what was it?
Pax Romana: Roman golden age (27 BC to 180). It was during this period that the Roman Empire achieved its greatest territorial extent under Trajan in 117.
The fifth governor of Roman Judaea under Tiberius, he presided over the trial of Jesus — and is so central to Christianity that he's named in both the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds; who is he?
Pontius Pilate: Roman governor of Judea and condemner of Jesus.
The favorite of Jacob's two wives and mother of Joseph and Benjamin, her older sister Leah was Jacob's first wife — who is she?
Also called Nagorno-Karabakh, this breakaway state in the South Caucasus governed land internationally recognized as Azerbaijan's until a 2023 offensive emptied it of its people — what was it?
Republic of Artsakh: Breakaway state in the South Caucasus (1991–2023). The conflict erupted into a full-out war in 1992.
A Yale graduate and Harvard Law alum, this former Navy lawyer to SEAL Team One became Florida's 46th governor and briefly ran for the 2024 Republican nomination — who is he?
Ron DeSantis: Governor of Florida since 2019.
In Buddhism it caps the Noble Eightfold Path, and in the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali it's the eighth and final limb of Ashtanga Yoga — what meditative state is this?
Samadhi: State of meditative consciousness. Samādhi (Pali and Sanskrit: समाधि), in the Indian religions, is a state of meditative consciousness.
Founded in 312 BC by one of Alexander the Great's generals, this Hellenistic Greek state stretched from Anatolia to Afghanistan before Pompey folded it into Rome — which state was it?
Seleucid Empire: Hellenistic state in West Asia (312–63 BC)
Nicknamed "the firebrand," this radical feminist helped found three New York organizations and in 1968 staged a symbolic "Burial of Traditional Womanhood" — who was she?

In July 1995, more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed in and around a town the UN had declared a 'safe area' — an event now recognized as the first legally proven genocide in Europe since World War II. What is it called?
Srebrenica massacre: 1995 genocidal killing of Bosniak Muslim men.

Widely regarded as one of the greatest Roman historians, this writer chronicled the empire from Augustus's death to Domitian's reign in two major works, and also penned an account of his general father-in-law's campaigns in Britain — who was he?

Beginning in 73 BCE with about 70 gladiators escaping a school in Capua, this slave revolt swelled to 120,000 people and became the only such uprising to directly threaten the Roman heartland — what was it called?
Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula
Third Servile War: 73–71 BCE Roman slave rebellion.
This second emperor of Vietnam's Trần dynasty handed the throne to his son yet stayed on as 'retired emperor,' co-commanding the victories that repelled two Mongol invasions of Đại Việt — who was he?
Trần Thánh Tông: Emperor of Đại Việt from 1258 to 1278.
Born in Turin, this ruler of Sardinia became the first king of a united Italy in 1861 and earned a nickname echoing an ancient Roman imperial title, 'Father of the Fatherland.' Who was he?
Victor Emmanuel II: King of Italy from 1861 to 1878.

Launched as Operation Enduring Freedom in response to the 9/11 attacks, this two-decade conflict began by toppling the Taliban-ruled Islamic Emirate with help from the Northern Alliance — what was it?
War in Afghanistan (2001–2021): U.S Armed conflict in South Asia.
A descendant of the Viking Rollo and once called 'the Bastard,' this Duke of Normandy won the Battle of Hastings in 1066 and became the first Norman king of England — who was he?
William the Conqueror: King of England from 1066 to 1087.

A former prosecutor general, he served the shortest term of any elected leader in his country's democratic history before removal in 2025 — and is now serving life for leading an insurrection. Which South Korean president is it?
Yoon Suk Yeol: President of South Korea from 2022 to 2025.
Who among these four was born earliest?
William Smith (geologist) (born 1769) is the earliest of the four. Financially ruined, Smith spent time in debtors' prison.
Which of these people was born first?
Levi Strauss (born 1829) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these was born first?
Eratosthenes (born 276 BC) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was established earliest?
Python (programming language) (founded 1991) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these is an astronomer?
Henrietta Swan Leavitt is an astronomer. Henrietta Swan Leavitt (July 4, 1868 – December 12, 1921) was an American astronomer.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
Augustus De Morgan is a mathematician. Augustus De Morgan (27 June 1806 – 18 March 1871) was a British mathematician and logician.
What is the atomic number of Technetium?
Technetium is a chemical element; it has symbol Tc and atomic number 43.
What is the atomic number of Sulfur?
Sulfur (American spelling or sulphur (Commonwealth spelling) is a chemical element; it has symbol S and atomic number 16.
In what year was Paul Allen born?
Paul Allen: Paul Gardner Allen (January 21, 1953 – October 15, 2018) was an American businessman, computer programmer, and investor.
In what year was Arthur Schopenhauer born?
Arthur Schopenhauer (22 February 1788 – 21 September 1860) was a German philosopher and writer.
In what year was Lex Fridman born?
Lex Fridman: Alexei "Lex" Fridman (born 15 August 1983) is an American computer scientist and podcaster.
In what year did Mario Molina die?
Mario Molina: Mario José Molina-Pasquel Henríquez (19 March 1943 – 7 October 2020) was a Mexican physical chemist.
In what year did Edward Teller die?
Edward Teller: Born in Austria-Hungary in 1908, Teller emigrated to the US in the 1930s, one of the many so-called "Martians", a group of Hungarian scientist émigrés.
In what year was Möbius strip discovered?
Möbius strip: In mathematics, a Möbius strip, Möbius band, or Möbius loop is a surface that can be formed by attaching the ends of a strip of paper together with a half-twist.
R (programming language): Robert Gentleman. R is a programming language for statistical computing and data visualization.
Prunus domestica: People's Republic of China. Prunus domestica is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae.
In which country is IAI Kfir?
Who is credited with discovering Eta Carinae?
Eta Carinae: Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser. It became the second-brightest star in the night sky between 11–14 March 1843 before fading well below naked-eye visibility after 1856.
Who is credited with discovering Benzene?
Benzene: Michael Faraday. Benzene is an organic chemical compound with the molecular formula C6H6.
Who is credited with discovering Vanadium?
Vanadium: Andrés Manuel del Río. Vanadium is a chemical element; it has symbol V and atomic number 23.

This British Formula One engineer, widely regarded as one of the sport's greatest designers, has served as technical chief at Williams, McLaren, and Red Bull, and now co-owns Aston Martin's F1 team — who is he?
Adrian Newey (born 26 December 1958) is a British engineer, aerodynamicist, automotive designer, and motorsport executive.

Caused by brain damage, disease, or sometimes sedative drugs, this condition splits into a retrograde type that erases memories before an event and an anterograde type that blocks new ones from forming — what is it called?
Amnesia is a deficit in memory caused by brain damage or brain diseases, but it can also be temporarily caused by the use of various sedative and hypnotic drugs.

Sitting at the milder end of a spectrum of diminished motivation — less severe than abulia and far short of akinetic mutism — this is a state marked by an absence of feeling, interest, or concern. What is it?
Apathy is a lack of feeling, emotion, interest, and/or concern about something.
Originally built by Hawker Siddeley and still produced under license in India today, this subsonic British trainer aircraft equips the Red Arrows aerobatic team — which jet?
BAE Systems Hawk is a British single-engine, subsonic, jet-powered advanced trainer aircraft.

This scientific discipline, a hybrid of chemistry and biology, studies the chemical processes occurring within living organisms and is generally divided into structural biology, enzymology, and metabolism — what's the field called?
Biochemistry (distinct from chemical biology), is the study of chemical processes within and relating to living organisms.
Present in both sexes from the same embryonic tissue, these two prominences on the upper torso permanently enlarge only in human females at puberty, driven by estrogen and growth hormone - name them?
Breast are two prominences located on the upper ventral region of the torso in humans and other primates.
Discovered in 1940, this non-intoxicating compound extracted from cannabis is used medically as an anticonvulsant for two rare, severe forms of childhood epilepsy — what is it?
Cannabidiol (CBD) is a phytocannabinoid, one of 113 identified cannabinoids in Cannabis, along with tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), and accounts for up to 40% of the plant's extract.
First cultivated in Mesoamerica and later spread worldwide during the Columbian Exchange, this edible gourd-family plant is also known as christophine, mirliton, or choko — what is it?

Chayote (previously placed in the obsolete genus Sechium, now in the genus Sicyos, as Sicyos edulis), also known as christophine, mirliton, gisquil, and choko, is an edible plant belonging to the gourd family, Cucurbitaceae.
Its glorious blue in glass and paint was long wrongly blamed on bismuth, and frustrated miners named its ore after a goblin. Which hard, gray element carries the symbol Co?
Cobalt is a chemical element; it has symbol Co and atomic number 27.
Which vanilla-scented, benzopyrone lactone compound acts as a plant's chemical defense against predators and, via its derivatives, gave rise to the anticoagulant warfarin?
Coumarin is an aromatic organic chemical compound with formula C9H6O2.
The word names both a noun — a plan or proposal made by a thinking agent — and a verb for developing one, always aiming to satisfy goals while weighing function and aesthetics; what is it?
Design is the concept or proposal for an object, process, or system.
Most of the 68 species sharing this name live in Eurasia and Africa, with only two found in North America — and "true" ones are merely a subfamily; what bird is it?
Eagle is the common name for certain large birds of prey within the family of the Accipitridae.
This Ancient Greek polymath, who became chief librarian at the Library of Alexandria, is considered the founder of geography as a discipline and coined much of its early terminology — who is he?

First recognised in the 1950s but not formally defined until 1990, this disorder of widespread chronic pain — often with fatigue and memory trouble — has no known cause and is treated multidisciplinarily. What is it?
Fibromyalgia (FM) is a long-term condition characterised by widespread chronic pain.
With about 37 species ranging from central Canada down to Costa Rica, this slender, keeled-scaled reptile typically sports longitudinal stripes in blue, yellow, or red — which reptile is it?
Garter snake is the common name for small to medium-sized snakes belonging to the genus Thamnophis in the family Colubridae.
This applied art and academic discipline uses text and images to craft visual communications aimed at specific audiences and objectives — what field is it?
Graphic design is a profession, academic discipline and applied art that involves creating visual communications intended to transmit specific messages to social groups, with specific objectives.
Credited with putting middle-class Americans behind the wheel, this industrialist lent his surname to the very philosophy of assembly-line manufacturing. Who is he?
Henry Ford (July 30, 1863 - April 7, 1947) was an American industrialist and business magnate.
Classified under sleep-wake disorders in the DSM-5, this condition causes a lack of alertness during waking hours despite — or because of — too much sleep. What is it?
Hypersomnia is a neurological disorder of excessive time spent sleeping or excessive sleepiness.
Whose 1687 book Principia Mathematica achieved the first great unification in physics and established classical mechanics?

Nicknamed 'Marvellous Merchiston,' this Scottish laird and mathematician popularised the decimal point and invented a set of calculating 'bones' — but he's best known for discovering what underlies the slide rule. Who was he?
John Napier (Latinized as Ioannes Neper; 1 February 1550 - 4 April 1617), nicknamed Marvellous Merchiston, was a Scottish landowner known as a mathematician, physicist and astronomer.
When the natural curve of the thoracic spine exceeds about 45 degrees, doctors give this excessive rounding of the upper back a name rooted in the Greek word for 'hump' — what is it?
Kyphosis (from Greek (kyphos) 'hump') is an abnormally excessive convex curvature of the spine as it occurs in the thoracic and sacral regions.
Born in 1880, this Australian therapist and part-time stage actor is remembered for coaching a stammering British monarch — who is he?
Lionel Logue (26 February 1880 - 12 April 1953) was an Australian speech and language therapist and amateur stage actor who helped King George VI manage his stammer.

An engineer and teacher from a poor family who once served as mayor of Tehran, this politician became Iran's sixth president in 2005 and was a fierce proponent of the country's nuclear program — who is he?
Mahmoud Ahmadinejad (n Sabbaghian; born 28 October 1956) is an Iranian politician who served as the sixth president of Iran from 2005 to 2013.
This natural biological transition marks the permanent end of menstrual periods, typically occurring between ages 45 and 55 as estrogen levels decline — what is it?
Menopause is the time when menstrual periods permanently stop, marking the end of the reproductive stage for the female human.

Caused by a poxvirus spread through direct contact, this viral skin infection produces small raised pink lesions with a distinctive dimple in the center, usually clearing on its own within a year — name the condition?
Molluscum contagiosum (MC), sometimes called water warts, is a viral infection of the skin that results in small raised pink lesions with a dimple in the center.
This flexible body part lets the head turn in every direction while its compartments guard the spinal cord and upper airway between head and torso — what is it, also known as the cervix?
Neck is the part of the body in many vertebrates that connects the head to the torso.
This insect order includes dragonflies and damselflies, the bulkier ones holding wings out at rest while the slender ones fold theirs along the body — what is it?
Odonata is an order of predatory flying insects that includes the dragonflies and damselflies (as well as the Epiophlebia damsel-dragonflies).
Contrasted with 'normophilic' interests and famously tallied at up to 549 types by Anil Aggrawal, this contested clinical category covers atypical sexual attraction — what's its name?
Paraphilia is an uncommon, intense, and persistent sexual arousal or attraction to anything not sexual by nature, though preference is favored for specific designations.
Written by the Hong sisters, this South Korean series about young mages dealing with heaven and earth aired on tvN in two parts during 2022 and 2023. What show is it?
Pharynx (pl.: pharynges) is the part of the throat behind the mouth and nasal cavity, and above the esophagus and trachea (the tubes going down to the stomach and the lungs respectively).
Cough, chest pain, fever, and trouble breathing point to this infection of the lungs' alveoli, often classified by where it was caught — community or hospital — what is it?
Pneumonia is an inflammatory condition of the lung primarily affecting the small air sacs known as alveoli.
This rose-family genus of roughly 340 species includes almonds, apricots, and cherries, whose pit encloses a kernel that's edible in some species and poisonous in others — which genus?

Prunus is a genus of flowering trees and shrubs from the family Rosaceae, with about 340 accepted species (as of March 2024) that include peaches and nectarines, apricots, plums, cherries and almonds.
Physicists denote this stretching of light's wavelength — caused by relative motion, gravity, or cosmic expansion — with the symbol z; its opposite is called blueshift. What is it?
Redshift is an increase in the wavelength, or equivalently, a decrease in the frequency, of electromagnetic radiation (such as light).

Grown mainly from Eastern and Northern Europe into Russia, this cold-tolerant grain crop is a member of the wheat tribe and its vigorous growth suppresses weeds while providing early forage for animals — name it?
Rye (Secale cereale) is a grass grown extensively as a grain, a cover crop and a forage crop.
This Soviet rocket engineer led the early development of his country's space program and designed the R-7, the world's first intercontinental ballistic missile — who is he?
Sergei Korolev was Soviet aerospace engineer (1907–1966).

Born in the Bronx to Puerto Rican parents and raised by her mother after her father's death, this Princeton grad became the third woman on the U.S. Supreme Court after Barack Obama's 2009 appointment — name this justice?
Sonia Sotomayor (born June 25, 1954) is an American lawyer and jurist who serves as an associate justice of the Supreme Court of the United States.
This small nocturnal marsupial sails between trees on membranes stretched from wrist to ankle, and its Latin name translates as 'short-headed rope-dancer' — what animal is it?
Sugar glider (Petaurus breviceps) is a small, omnivorous, arboreal, and nocturnal gliding possum.

This family of marine and freshwater fish can inflate themselves dramatically, revealing thin spines that stay hidden against their skin until they puff up — unlike their spinier, porcupine-like relatives — name this fish family?
Tetraodontidae is a family of marine and freshwater fish in the order Tetraodontiformes.

Stretching from the base of the skull down to the lower back and out to each shoulder blade, this large paired muscle supports the arm and moves the scapula in three distinct ways — what's the muscle?
Trapezius is a large paired trapezoid-shaped surface muscle that extends longitudinally from the occipital bone to the lower thoracic vertebrae of the spine and laterally to the spine of the scapula.
Native only to the wetlands of the Carolinas, which carnivorous plant snaps shut a 'jaw' formed from the tips of its leaves when an insect trips it?
Venus flytrap (Dionaea muscipula) is a carnivorous plant native to the temperate and subtropical wetlands of North Carolina and South Carolina, on the East Coast of the United States.
This noble gas, found in trace amounts in Earth's atmosphere, powers arc lamps, serves as a rare anesthetic, and was the first of its family coaxed into a genuine chemical compound — which element?
Xenon is a chemical element; it has symbol Xe and atomic number 54.
Unearthed in Montana by Jack Horner's team in 1987, this 20-foot horned dinosaur sported a bony neck-frill and lived roughly 75 million years ago — which species?
Achelousaurus: Genus of ceratopsid dinosaur from North America.
Often called the father of theoretical computer science, this Englishman gave us a famous 'machine' that formalized the very idea of computation — who was he?

Nicknamed 'lazy eye,' this childhood vision disorder occurs when the brain favors one eye over the other, and correcting the underlying cause doesn't restore sight right away — what is this condition?
Amblyopia: Failure of the brain to process input from one eye.
Comprising over 22,000 species including ragworms, earthworms, and leeches, this phylum of segmented worms use parapodia to move — what is it?
Annelid: Phylum of segmented worms. The basic annelid form consists of multiple segments called metameres.
Known commonly as palms, this family of over 2,600 flowering plant species includes climbers, shrubs, and tree-like forms mostly found in the tropics — what's the family called?
Arecaceae: Palm family of flowering plants.

Despite its name being something of a misnomer, this herding dog breed was developed in California and takes its name from imported collies that arrived alongside sheep from Down Under — what breed is it?
Australian Shepherd: American breed of dog. The Australian Shepherd, also known as the Aussie, is a breed of herding dog from the United States.
Making up nearly 40% of all known insects with around 400,000 described species, this order is distinguished by front wings hardened into protective cases called elytra — what creatures are these?
Beetle: Order of insects. Over 300 species are used as food, mostly as larvae; species widely consumed include mealworms and rhinoceros beetle larvae.
This small Old World flycatcher breeds in rocky habitats from the British Isles to Morocco and central China, staying put in milder areas but migrating from colder ones — what bird is it?
Black redstart: Species of bird. The black redstart (Phoenicurus ochruros) is a small passerine bird in the Old World flycatcher family.
Formed from the C5-T1 spinal nerve roots, this network of nerves runs through the neck and over the first rib to supply the shoulder, arm, and hand — what is it?
Brachial plexus: Network of nerves. This plexus extends from the spinal cord, through the cervicoaxillary canal in the neck, over the first rib, and into the armpit.
Developed in 1964 at Britain's Royal Radar Establishment and influenced by JOVIAL, this programming language was chosen by the UK Ministry of Defence in 1971 for military applications — what is it?
CORAL: Early programming language. The R was originally for "radar", not "real-time".
Derived from Greek words for 'heart' and 'study,' this branch of internal medicine covers coronary artery disease, heart failure, and electrophysiology — which medical field?
Cardiology: Branch of medicine dealing with the heart.
Triggered by anything from a stroke to a bout of altitude sickness, this dangerous buildup of fluid inside the skull raises pressure on brain tissue and can cause seizures or worse — what is it?
Cerebral edema: Excess accumulation of fluid in the brain.
This class of jawed fish — including sharks, rays, skates, and ghost-like chimaeras — has skeletons made entirely of cartilage rather than bone — what is it called?
Chondrichthyes: Class of jawed cartilaginous fish. Chondrichthyes are aquatic vertebrates with paired fins, paired nares, placoid scales, and conus arteriosus in the heart.
Recognizable by a prominent crest and curved bill, this Australasian parrot family includes 21 species, the smallest of which is the cockatiel — which family of birds?
Cockatoo: Any bird in the family Cacatuidae.
What is this — “Animal sexual reproductive act in which a male introduces sperm into the female's body”?

Copulation (zoology): Animal sexual reproductive act in which a male introduces sperm into the female's body. In zoology, copulation is animal sexual behavior in which a male introduces sperm into the female's body, especially directly into the female's reproductive tract.
This medical sign turns the lips, nail beds, and ear lobes a bluish-purple hue when blood isn't carrying enough oxygen, and comes in central and peripheral forms — what is it called?
Cyanosis: Decreased oxygen in the blood. Cyanosis is apparent usually in the body tissues covered with thin skin, including the mucous membranes, lips, nail beds, and ear lobes.
Often called eczema, this term covers skin inflammation marked by itchiness, redness and rash — sometimes with tiny blisters, sometimes thickening over time. What is it?
Dermatitis: Inflammatory disease of the skin.

Developed in the early 1950s to replace the propeller-driven Skyraider, this US Navy carrier jet had a maximum takeoff weight of just 24,500 pounds — about half the Navy's specification — which aircraft?
Douglas A-4 Skyhawk: Carrier-based attack aircraft.

This Russian political scientist studies authoritarian governance and legislative process, taught at Moscow institutions for nearly a decade, and by 2022 had a YouTube channel with a million subscribers — who is she?
Dubbed 'the father of nuclear physics,' this New Zealander won a Nobel Prize in Chemistry despite proposing that atoms have a tiny, densely charged nucleus — who is he?
Ernest Rutherford: New Zealand physicist and chemist (1871–1937)
Beloved in gardens for gobbling up pests, this spiny mammal native to Iberia and Scandinavia was introduced to New Zealand in the late 1800s but is now Red Listed in Britain — what is it?
European hedgehog: Species of small spiny mammal.
Native to the Mediterranean and grown since ancient times, this teardrop-shaped fruit is technically a syconium and comes from the type species of a genus with over 800 members — what fruit is it?
Fig: Species of flowering plant, or its fruit.
This British-American theoretical physicist lent his name to a hypothetical genetically engineered 'tree' and a transform used in additive number theory — who was he?
Freeman Dyson: British theoretical physicist and mathematician (1923–2020)
This mathematician founded set theory and proved that there are more real numbers than natural numbers, revealing an infinity of infinities — who is he?
Known online by the alias 'anakata,' this Swedish computer specialist co-founded a notorious BitTorrent site and later helped WikiLeaks with its 2010 release of a leaked military video — who is he?
Gottfrid Svartholm: Swedish computer specialist. Parts of an interview with Svartholm commenting on the May 2006 police raid of The Pirate Bay are featured in Good Copy Bad Copy and Steal This Film.
Nicknamed the slime eel, this jawless marine scavenger is the only living animal with a skull but no proper backbone — what is it?
Hagfish: Class of eel-shaped, slime-producing animal.

Famous for the ideas of "bounded rationality" and "satisficing," this remarkable scholar won both a Turing Award and a Nobel in Economics — bridging computer science, economics, and psychology. Who was he?
Herbert A. Simon: American academic and Nobel Laureate (1916–2001)

Found only in the Americas from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego, these roughly 375 species pull off rapid, maneuverable flight thanks to an exceptional metabolism — and their males flaunt the widest plumage diversity of any bird — what are they?
This Russian-American engineer built the first successful four-engine aircraft in 1913 and went on to pioneer the modern helicopter — who was he?
Nicknamed 'Dr. Death,' this pathologist assisted at least 130 patients in dying and was convicted of murder after broadcasting one such case on television — who is he?
Jack Kevorkian: American pathologist and euthanasia activist (1928–2011)
The youngest division chief in GM history shepherded the Pontiac GTO before founding the motor company behind a stainless-steel sports car immortalized in Back to the Future — who was he?
John DeLorean: American automobile engineer and executive (1925–2005)
Sold under names like Toradol and Acular, this NSAID's use is capped at five days due to serious side-effect risk, with relief starting within an hour — what drug is it?
Described both as a science and as the art of justice, this set of enforced rules can be made by legislatures, executive decrees or judges' precedent — what is it?
A sweet, aromatic flavouring used in confectionery, tobacco, and pharmaceuticals comes from the root of which legume — though more than a couple of milligrams per kilo a day can cause trouble?
Often a complication of cancer treatment, this incurable, progressive swelling condition is managed with compression therapy and manual drainage rather than diuretics — what is it?
Lymphedema: Swelling due to a compromised lymphatic system.

The first woman to write a mathematics handbook and the first appointed as a university math professor, this Milanese scholar later traded calculus for four decades of theology and charity — who is she?
Maria Gaetana Agnesi: Italian mathematician and philanthropist (1718–1799)
Triggered by falling progesterone, this regular discharge from the uterine lining signals that pregnancy hasn't occurred, and typically first arrives at menarche between ages 11 and 13 — what is it?
Menstruation: Periodic shedding of the uterine lining.
Nicknamed 'Foxbat' by NATO and built largely from stainless steel, this Soviet interceptor still holds the altitude record for an airbreathing piloted aircraft at 38 km — which jet?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25: Family of interceptor and reconnaissance aircraft.
Grown to feed silkworms for commercial silk production, this fast-growing tree releases its pollen at more than half the speed of sound — which species?
Morus alba: Plant species in the fig family.
Divided in two by a central septum, this air-filled space sits behind the nose and forms the uppermost part of the respiratory system — what is it?
Nasal cavity: Large, air-filled space above and behind the nose in the middle of the face.
A catecholamine whose very name nods to the kidney, it acts as both a hormone and neurotransmitter and is called "noradrenaline" outside the US — what is it?
Norepinephrine: Catecholamine hormone and neurotransmitter. The general function of norepinephrine is to mobilize the brain and body for action.
Discovered by naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace in 1859, this fungus hijacks carpenter ants' brains and marches them down to the forest floor before killing them — which organism?

Ophiocordyceps unilateralis: Species of fungus. Ophiocordyceps unilateralis, commonly known as zombie-ant fungus, is an insect-pathogenic fungus, discovered by the British naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace in 1859.
First domesticated in Mesoamerica and led in production today by India, this tropical fruit belongs to the small genus Carica — what is it?
Papaya: Species of tropical fruit plant.
Derived from the Latin for 'by a hundred,' this dimensionless number expresses a ratio as a fraction of 100 and is usually written with a % sign — what is it called?

Percentage: Number or ratio expressed as a fraction of 100. In mathematics, a percentage, percent, or per cent (from Latin per centum 'by a hundred') is a number or ratio expressed as a fraction of 100.
This healthcare profession uses patient education and hands-on interventions to prevent, treat, and restore mobility, with specialties from sports medicine to pediatrics — which field?
Physical therapy: Profession that helps a disabled person function in everyday life.
Built from many linked simple sugars and including starch, glycogen, and cellulose among its examples, this class of carbohydrate is the most abundant in our food — what is it called?
Polysaccharide: Long carbohydrate polymers such as starch, glycogen, cellulose, and chitin.
Known by folk names like 'bird cherry' and 'Mayday tree,' this flowering plant in the rose family is native to Europe and northern Asia — what species is it?
Prunus padus: Species of flowering plant in the rose family.
What term describes an atom, molecule, or ion with at least one unpaired valence electron, making it highly reactive and prone to processes like dimerization or polymerization?
Radical (chemistry): Atom, molecule, or ion that has an unpaired valence electron; typically highly reactive.
Named from Greek words for 'rose' and 'tree,' this flowering shrub genus is Nepal's national flower and includes azaleas as a subgenus — which plant?
Rhododendron: Genus of flowering plants. Azaleas make up two subgenera of Rhododendron.
This Japanese botanist lived and worked during the Meiji era of the late 19th century — who was he?
Ryōkichi Yatabe: Japanese botanist and poet. Ryōkichi Yatabe (矢田部良吉; October 13, 1851 – August 8, 1899) was a Japanese botanist during the Meiji era.
Sitting near the center of the Milky Way between Libra and Sagittarius, this zodiac constellation's recognition predates ancient Greek culture — which constellation?
Scorpius: Zodiac constellation in the southern celestial hemisphere.
Resembling a long-nosed mouse but actually a closer relative of hedgehogs and moles, this small mammal has sharp spike-like teeth rather than gnawing incisors — what is it?
Mostly made from potato starch but also found in apples and berries, this slowly-metabolized sugar alcohol is an isomer of mannitol, differing only at one hydroxyl group. What is it?

In probability theory, this mathematical concept models a family of random variables indexed often by time, used to describe things like bacterial growth or a gas molecule's erratic path — what is it called?
Stochastic process: Collection of random variables. Stochastic processes are widely used as mathematical models of systems and phenomena that appear to vary in a random manner.
This medical term describes a resting heart rate that exceeds 100 beats per minute — what is it?
Tachycardia: Heart rate exceeding normal resting rate.
Native to the tropical Americas, this small evergreen tree's fermented seeds become cocoa powder, cocoa butter, and chocolate — which tree?
